summary: The cryptographic algorithm and key size requirements set when DKIM was designed a decade earlier had become obsolete. This document updates the requirements to what is minimally suitable for use with currently specified algorithms.

eli5.summary: The locks that protected email signatures long ago had become too weak. This says to use stronger ones.

questions: what rsa key size should dkim use
subtitle: DKIM signers must use rsa-sha256 and keys of at least 1024 bits; rsa-sha1 is retired.

tldr.problem: The algorithm and key size rules in DKIM were set about a decade earlier and had become functionally obsolete, with short keys weakening the protocol and SHA-1 considered weak.
tldr.mechanism: Signers MUST use rsa-sha256 and RSA keys of at least 1024 bits (2048 recommended). rsa-sha1 MUST NOT be used, and verifiers must not accept keys under 1024 bits.
tldr.outcome: The update changes the DKIM rules in RFC 6376 and marks the sha1 hash as historic in the IANA registry.

today: RFC 8301 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6376. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Old DKIM Crypto
sections.content:
DKIM signs email by hashing the message headers and content and signing the header hash with a digital signature. Recipients fetch the verification key from the DNS, where it is stored in a TXT record. The defining document, RFC 6376, specified a single signing algorithm, RSA, and recommended key sizes of 1024 to 2048 bits, while still requiring verification of 512-bit keys.

The operational community had recognized that shorter keys compromise the effectiveness of DKIM. Widely used DNS configuration software handles only a single 256-octet string in a TXT record, which puts a practical limit on key sizes because RSA keys significantly longer than 1024 bits do not fit.
sections.eli5: Email gets a signature so you can tell it is real. The signing locks were old and some were too small to be safe, so it was time to upgrade them.

sections.title: Signing and Verification Algorithms
sections.content:
DKIM defines two algorithms, rsa-sha1 and rsa-sha256. Signers MUST sign using rsa-sha256, and verifiers MUST be able to verify using it. rsa-sha1 MUST NOT be used for signing or verifying.

The reasons given are the recognized weakness of the SHA-1 hash and the wide availability of SHA-256, which has been a required part of DKIM since it was standardized in 2007. The change is made now to give the operational community time to shift before any SHA-1-related crisis. Signatures made with a historic algorithm have permanently failed evaluation.
sections.eli5: There were two ways to scramble the message for signing, and one was getting weak. Everyone must now use the stronger one.

sections.title: Key Sizes
sections.content:
The RFC calls key size a trade-off between cost, performance and risk. Signers MUST use RSA keys of at least 1024 bits and SHOULD use keys of at least 2048 bits.

Verifiers MUST be able to validate signatures with keys from 1024 bits to 4096 bits, and MAY be able to handle larger ones. Verifiers MUST NOT treat signatures using RSA keys of less than 1024 bits as valid. Such signatures, for example rsa-sha256 with less than 1024 bits, have permanently failed evaluation. Verifier policies can use key length as one measure of whether a signature is acceptable.
sections.eli5: A longer key is like a lock with more pins, which is harder to pick. Tiny locks are no longer accepted, and big ones are encouraged.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The document does not change the Security Considerations of RFC 6376. It reduces the risk of signature compromise from weak cryptography, and the SHA-1 risks in RFC 6194 are resolved because rsa-sha1 is no longer used by DKIM.

IANA updated the sha1 entry in the "DKIM Hash Algorithms" registry so that its references are RFC 6376 and RFC 8301 and its status is historic.
sections.eli5: Dropping the weak lock makes fake signatures harder. The official list of locks now marks the old one as retired.

cells: MUST be 1024 bits or more; SHOULD be 2048 bits or more
MUST handle 1024 to 4096 bits; keys under 1024 are invalid
